title: Lost, or separated from your group: what to do (from the Army cold-weather and survival manuals)
asks: i am lost what do i do
lost in the woods what now
we got separated from our group
should i stay put or keep walking if lost
lost hiker what to do first
lost in a snowstorm with my group
do i stay where i am or try to walk out
im lost wat do i do
we are lost, no trail, getting dark, what do we do, over
answer: Keep calm and think clearly. Survival depends upon clear thinking and resourcefulness. Try to help each other.

Do not decide anything right away. The Army survival manual says to avoid making any decision immediately after it happens: if possible, wait until the shock has subsided, then evaluate the situation and decide. Ask whether a head injury or other condition is affecting anyone's ability to make a clear decision.

Staying put or moving is a decision that requires careful consideration. Before any move, weigh the Army survival manual's factors. Does this place provide adequate food, water and shelter, and a way to report, communicate or support the effort to recover you? Does an injury or circumstance limit anyone's ability to move? Are the tools, equipment and materials needed to support the move available? Moving is risky unless you have the necessities of survival, and leaving a safe shelter to travel in adverse weather is foolhardy (the manual's only exception, written for soldiers, is an escape or evasion situation).

Then decide whether to stay or move, knowing that the sources differ. This library has no civilian search-and-rescue guidance for lost hikers: what it has on being lost comes from Army manuals. The Army cold-weather manual, written for soldiers separated from their unit, says: if all is quiet and nothing guides you back, go back to the last known position; if that is not possible, carefully consider the journey already made, and the distance and direction from the starting point. The Army survival manual says: where the authorities are in control and are willing and able to help recover you, that may favor staying near the place where you became isolated, at first; consider moving only when you are certain that water, shelter, food and help can be reached, or when, after waiting several days, you are convinced that rescue is not coming and you are equipped to travel.

If you are with others, gather information from the group. (The cold-weather manual then has a military unit send out search parties, marking their trail, while the rest of the group seeks shelter. That is a procedure for units and is not given here as a step.)
If you stay, or cannot find any known location: stay together. Meet the emergency as a group, do not wander off as individuals, and never let anyone straggle.
Take shelter. If a tent is available, set it up and get in. If there is no tent, build an improvised shelter. The type of shelter is not important if it protects from the weather.

Keep warm. If lost in a forest, light a fire. If lost where there are no trees, do not use a gasoline stove to heat the shelter: use it only to prepare hot food and drinks, conserve the fuel supply, and get into the sleeping bag to stay warm.
Check the food supply: collect all the food and water in the group and ration it systematically.

Check communications. If there is a radio, use it to call for help. In a forest, prepare fires to attract search planes: smoke is better by day and flame is better at night. Mirrors and ground signals help attract search parties.
Rest: less energy is expended. Eat while resting.
Watch each other for cold injury, using the buddy system. Watch for signs of frostbite and hypothermia.
If you are trapped in a vehicle in a winter storm: FEMA says to stay in your vehicle.

quotes.text: Survival depends upon clear thinking and resourcefulness: Keep calm. Think. Try to help each other. Stay together. Keep warm.

Does the isolated person have a head injury or condition that effects their ability to make a clear decision? Avoid making any decision immediately after the isolating event. If possible, wait a period to allow for recovery from the mental (if not the physical) shock resulting from the event. When shock has subsided, evaluate the situation, analyze the factors involved, and make valid decisions.
The decision to stay in place or move while isolated requires careful consideration. The reasons to stay in place or move are typically based upon the following:

Mission orders should contain isolated Soldier guidance. This is detailed instructions for what to do if separated from the unit. A Soldier can be separated from the main troop body, especially when fighting in action.

If all is quiet and there are no battle sounds or aircraft for guidance to friendly lines, go back to the last known position. If that is not possible, carefully consider the journey already made and the distance and direction from the starting point.

An operational environment in which host country military and law enforcement agencies have control as well as the intent and capability to assist recovery operations may favor staying near the isolation site (ex. aircraft crash) initially. Movement is considered only when certain that water, shelter, food, and help can be reached, or after having waited several days, they are convinced that recovery is not coming and they are equipped to travel.
The current location does not provide adequate food, water, shelter, or the ability to report/communicate or support the recovery effort.
Injury or circumstance that limits the ability (physical and mental) of the isolated person to move.

Are the necessary tools, equipment and materials available to support movement? Movement is risky unless the necessities of survival are available. To leave a safe shelter to travel in adverse weather conditions is foolhardy unless in an escape or evasion situation.

If with others, information should be gathered from the group. Send search parties out to find the next known steering mark. Carefully mark trails so the search party can return to guide the main group forward, or to rejoin the group should their search be unproductive. Meanwhile, the rest of the group should seek shelter. If the search party fails to find any known location, perform the steps below but remember to think clearly and keep calm:
Stay together: Meet the emergency as a group. Do not wander off as individuals, and never allow Soldiers to straggle.
Take shelter: If a tent is available, set it up and get in. If there is no tent, build an improvised shelter. The type of shelter is not important if there is protection from the weather.

Keep warm: If lost in a forest, light a fire (depending upon the enemy situation). If lost in an area where there are no trees, do not use the gasoline stove to heat the shelter. The stove is used only to prepare hot food and drinks. Conserve the fuel supply and get into the sleeping bag to stay warm.
Check the food supply: All food and water in the group is collected and rationed systematically.

Check communications: If there is a radio set, use it to contact the parent unit for help. If in a forest, prepare fires to attract search planes. Smoke is better by day and flame is better at night. Mirrors and ground signals are helpful in attracting search parties. Isolated Soldier guidance has ground and air signals for search planes. Rest: Less energy is expended. Food is eaten when resting.
Using the buddy system to watch for heat and cold injury.
Limit your time outside. If you need to go outside, wear layers of warm clothing. Watch for signs of frostbite and hypothermia. Avoid driving. If you are trapped, stay in your vehicle.

conflict: Stay or move (now shown side by side, attributed, in step 4, after ATP's decision factors in step 3 and before every other step): TC 21-3 (2025) para 7-3, written for a soldier separated from a unit in cold regions, says to 'go back to the last known position' when 'all is quiet and there are no battle sounds or aircraft for guidance to friendly lines'. ATP 3-50.21 (2018) para 7-1 says to avoid making any decision immediately, that an environment where host-country agencies have 'the intent and capability to assist recovery operations may favor staying near the isolation site', and that 'Movement is considered only when certain that water, shelter, food, and help can be reached, or after having waited several days'. FEMA P-2064 (2020, winter storm) says 'If you are trapped, stay in your vehicle.' The owner must decide whether to lead with one of them. ATP's sentence about host-country military and law enforcement is adapted on the card to 'the authorities are in control and are willing and able to help recover you', attributed to the Army survival manual. Unit procedure left out as a step, for the owner to decide: TC 21-3 para 7-4 'Send search parties out to find the next known steering mark. Carefully mark trails so the search party can return to guide the main group forward... Meanwhile, the rest of the group should seek shelter'; the card mentions it in step 5 as a procedure for military units, because for a small civilian group it clashes with the same manual's 'Do not wander off as individuals'. ATP 7-1's other factors are military (isolated Soldier guidance or evasion plan, enemy situation, escape routes) and are not shown; its exception 'unless in an escape or evasion situation' is shown labelled as written for soldiers. No civilian search-and-rescue guidance for lost hikers is in the kit (searched every document); step 4 says so.

review.notes: Pass. (1) All four previous findings fixed: ATP 3-50.21 7-1's decision factors now come before any movement step (step 3: food, water, shelter and a way to signal; injury; tools; leaving a safe shelter in adverse weather is 'foolhardy', with its escape-or-evasion exception labelled as written for soldiers); TC 21-3 7-3 ('go back to the last known position', labelled as written for soldiers separated from their unit) and ATP 7-1 (staying near the isolation site may be favoured at first; move only when certain water, shelter, food and help can be reached, or after waiting several days) are side by side and attributed in step 4; the unit search-party procedure (TC 21-3 7-4) is a labelled note, not a step; the adapted 'authorities are in control and willing and able' wording is attributed; the no-civilian-search-and-rescue gap is stated in step 4 (confirmed: FEMA P-2064 and the Idaho regulations hold no lost-person guidance; their 'lost' hits are place names). (2) Every line re-checked against TC 21-3 7-1..7-4, ATP 3-50.21 7-1 and the FEMA winter-storm bullets; the 'depending upon the enemy situation' clause is rightly dropped; 'Eat while resting' = 'Food is eaten when resting'. (3) Conflicts shown attributed. (4) Nothing safety-critical missing. (5) All asks answered (stay or move, separated, snowstorm, getting dark). (6) Protocol; lines are steps. Optional: step 2's 'Do not decide anything right away' follows ATP's 'Avoid making any decision immediately' literally, but ATP writes it about the stay-or-move decision; 'Do not decide right away whether to stay or move' would avoid it being read as 'do not take shelter yet'. previous review: (verdict fail, by claude-opus-5-5 xhigh) Fail. Drafter flag verdict (go back vs stay put vs stay in vehicle): the three sources answer different situations, and the card states them as unattributed steps that contradict each other. (1) Step 3 'go back to the last known position' is TC 21-3 7-3, written for a soldier with 'no battle sounds or aircraft for guidance to friendly lines'. ATP 3-50.21 7-1 says avoid any decision immediately after the event, that conditions may favour staying near the site at first, and to move only when water, shelter, food and help can be reached. The card gives the TC rule as step 3 and the ATP rule as the last line, both unattributed, so the reader is told to move first and to consider staying last. Fix: show both near the top, attributed and side by side ('The Army cold-weather manual, written for soldiers separated from their unit, says...; the Army survival manual says...'), and put ATP 7-1's decision factors before any movement step (the place lacks food, water, shelter or a way to signal; an injury limits movement; tools available; 'To leave a safe shelter to travel in adverse weather conditions is foolhardy'). (2) Step 4 'send a search party... the rest seek shelter' is a unit procedure (TC 21-3 7-4) and clashes with step 5 'do not wander off as individuals' for a small civilian group. Fix: label it as the cold-weather manual's procedure for units, or drop it; owner to decide. (3) The last line adapts ATP's 'host country military and law enforcement agencies have control as well as the intent and capability to assist recovery operations' to 'authorities are in control and willing and able to help recover you' - acceptable, but attribute it. (4) Honest gap: the kit has no civilian search-and-rescue guidance for lost hikers (said only in the conflict field); add a line saying so, since nearly every ask is a civilian hiker. Otherwise faithful: keep calm, stay together, shelter, keep warm (enemy-situation clause rightly dropped), no gasoline stove for heat, ration food and water, radio/fires/mirrors, rest, buddy system, FEMA winter-storm 'stay in your vehicle' attributed, blizzard warnings.
